abstract: Highlights • APOC1 is a key prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target in PTC. • Cyclopamine identified via Connectivity Map to target APOC1 pathways. • APOC1 deficiency synergizes with Cyclopamine for enhanced tumor suppression. • In vivo validation shows Cyclopamine effectively inhibits PTC growth.
methods:
Materials and methods
Cell culture
Human papillary thyroid carcinomas cell lines TPC-1 and B-CPAP were procured from Biotechnology Co., Ltd. Of cellcook (Guang Zhou, China). TPC-1 were cultivated in RPMI-1640 medium (Invitrogen, 11,875,093) with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Gibco, 10,099,141). B-CPAP were cultivated in RPMI-1640 medium (Invitrogen, 11,875,093) with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Gibco, 10,099,141), 1 % NEAA (Invitrogen 11,140,050), 1 % Glutamax (Invitrogen 35,050,061), 1 %Sodium Pyruvate 100 mM Solution (Invitrogen 11,360,070) and 100 U/ml penicillin/streptomycin at a temperature of 37 °C and 5 % CO2. Cyclopamine (APExBIO. A8340) and CCK-8 reagent were purchased from APExBIO.Edu (C0071S) were purchased from Beyotime.
Mouse model
All animal experiments were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Naval Medical University, Shanghai, China (approval ID: NMUMREC-2025–055). BALB/c mice aged 6 to 8 weeks used in the experiment were purchased from Shanghai Laboratory Animal Research Center (SLARC). A total of 2 × 10^
6
TPC-1 thyroid papillary carcinoma cells suspended in 0.2 mL PBS (PBS: Matrigel=1:1) were implanted subcutaneously into the right side of the mice. When the tumor volume reached 50 to 100 mm^
3
, the mice were randomly divided into four groups (five mice each group). The Cyclopamine treatment group was administered 25 mg/kg Cyclopamine via intraperitoneal injection every two days for 20 days. The control group received 0.9 % NaCl via intraperitoneal injection. Throughout the treatment period, the body weight and tumor size of each mouse were recorded every three days. Tumor volume was calculated using the formula
V
= (width)^
2
× length / 2. At the end of the experiment, the mice were euthanized, and the tumors and selected organ tissues were quickly separated and weighed.
CCK-8 assay
For cell proliferation assay, TPC-1 or B-CPAP cells (1 × 10
5
cells/well) were plated in 96-well plates exposed to different concentrations of Cyclopamine. At 0, 24, 48 and 72 h post-treatment, cells were collected and cell proliferation was evaluated by CCK-8 assay kit (Beyotime, China).
Colony formation assay
In each well of a 6-well plate, 1000 cells were seeded and treated with Cyclopamine (10 μM) or siAPOC1 sequences for 14 days. After 14 days of treatment, visible clones were observed. After fixation with 4 % paraformaldehyde (PFA) at room temperature for 30 min, cells were stained with crystal violet solution (Beyotime, China). The number of clones was counted, and images were collected.
Wound-healing assay
TPC-1 and B-CPAP cells into a 12-well plate. When the cell confluence reaches about 90 %, use a 20 μL pipette tip to create vertical scratches in the center of each well. Then, gently wash three times with PBS to remove the detached cells. Following the washing step, add siAPOC1 solution at the specified concentration to the wells and continue culturing the cells. Observe the changes in scratch widths by microscopy after 24 h to assess the effect of cell migration ability.
Apoptosis analysis
The apoptosis detection kit (MultiSciences BioTech) was used to evaluate the effects of Cyclopamine and siAPOC1 treatments on apoptosis in TPC-1 and B-CPAP cells. A suspension containing 1 × 10^6 cells was gently mixed with 5 μL Annexin V-FITC solution and 10 μL PI staining solution, then incubated in the dark on ice for 5 min. Fluorescence analysis was subsequently performed using flow cytometry.
Molecular docking
The structure of APOC1 protein comes from the RCSB PDB database (
https://www.pdbus.org/
), in PDB format. Farnesylthioacetic-acid; Papaverine; Hycanthone; Indolophenanthridine; Nicaraven; Methylnorlichexanthone; Fananserin and Cyclopamine. The three-dimensional structure comes from the PubChem database (
https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/
), in MOL2 file format. Molecular docking is performed using Autodock Vina software, evaluating the stability of the receptor and ligand binding through binding energy.
Real-time PCR (qRT-PCR)
Total RNA was extracted from cells using an RNA extraction kit (Fastagen). The RNA concentration was measured in ng/μL using a NanoDrop 2000 (Thermo Scientific). cDNA was synthesized using a reverse transcription kit (Accurate BioTech) for qPCR. Quantitative PCR detection was then performed using Fast qPCR Mix (Accurate BioTech, catalog number [please insert catalog number]). The expression levels of the target gene were normalized using GAPDH as an internal reference. The primer sequences used in this study are as follows:
APOC1
, forward primer: TCCAGTGCCTTGGATAAGCTG; reverse primer: GGCTGATGAGTTCCCGAGC;
GAPDH, forward primer: ACAACTTTGGTATCGTGGAAGG; reverse primer: GCCATCACGCCACAGTTTC.
Western blotting analysis
The harvested cells were lysed in cell lysis buffer (Beyeyotime, P0013B) to obtain a complete cell lysate. The protein concentration was evaluated using the BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Fisher, A55865). Equal amounts of protein from each sample were loaded for electrophoresis via SDS-PAGE. And proteins were transferred onto nitrocellulose (NC) membranes. Subsequently, the NC membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies APOC1 (Abcam, ab198288) and GAPDH (Proteintech, 6004). Followed by incubation secondary antibodies under appropriate conditions. Immunoreactive bands were analysis of the Western blot was using ImageJ software.
Transfection
For the
APOC1
knockdown experiment,
APOC1
siRNA was synthesized by Sangon Shanghai Technology. The sequences of
APOC1
siRNAs and negative control siRNAs are as follows: siAPOC1
#
1: GAAACACACUGGAGGACAATT,UUGUCCUCCAGUGUGUUUCTT; siAPOC1
#
2:CAUCAAAAGAGUGGAACUUTT,AAGUUCCACUCUUUUGAUGTT;siAPOC1
#
3:AGAAAGUGAAGGAAGAAACUTT,AGUUUCUUCCUUCACUUUCUTT; control siRNAs: forward primer UUCUCCGAACGUGUCACGUTT; reverse primer: ACGUGACACGUUCGGAGAATT. Briefly, cell culture was performed in a 6-well plate. After 12 h of cell culture, siRNA was transfected into the cells using the transfection reagent jet PRIME (catalog number 101,000,046).
Immunofluorescence
Using the EdU cell proliferation detection kit (Beyotime, China) to evaluate cell proliferation by detecting cell DNA synthesis. Cells were seeded at 5 × 10^
5
cells per well in a 12-well plate. Pre-warmed EdU (20 μM, 37 °C) was added to the culture medium, and incubation was performed for 2 h to complete EdU labeling. Subsequently, cells were fixed with 4 % paraformaldehyde (PFA) and permeabilized with Triton X-100 (Beyotime, China) for 20 min, followed by the addition of click reaction solution and Hoechst nuclear staining. Quantitative analysis of EdU-positive cells was performed using a confocal laser scanning microscope imaging system (CLSM600, China).
Using the Ki-67 cell proliferation detection kit (Beyotime, China), cells were seeded at 5 × 10^5 cells per well in a 12-well plate, fixed with 4 % paraformaldehyde (PFA) and permeabilized with Triton X-100 for 20 min, and then blocked with 10 % blocking solution at room temperature for 0.5 h. Subsequently, the cells were incubated overnight with the primary antibody Ki-67 antibody at 4 °C. The cells were stained with Alexa Fluor 647 labeled secondary antibody (Proteintech) and counterstained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) (
D21490
, Thermo Fisher) for the nuclei. Quantitative analysis of Ki-67 positive cells was performed using a confocal microscopy imaging system (CLSM600, China).
Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 20.0 and GraphPad Prism 10, Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) from at least three independent experiments. Comparisons between multiple groups were conducted using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s post hoc test. For non-normal data, nonparametric tests, such as the Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn’s post hoc test, were applied. Differences were considered statistically significant at
P
< 0.05, denoted as *
P
< 0.05, **
P
< 0.01, and *
P
< 0.001. Correlation analyses between experimental outcomes, docking binding energies, and gene expression levels were performed using Pearson or Spearman correlation coefficients, depending on data distribution.
body:
Introduction
The global incidence of thyroid cancer continues to rise each year, accounting for approximately 3 % of all cancer cases worldwide [
[1]
,
[2]
,
[3]
]. Moreover, this disease increasingly affects younger individuals [
[4]
,
[5]
,
[6]
]. Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) represents the most common subtype of thyroid cancer and is the predominant form of differentiated thyroid carcinoma (DTC) [
7
]. Although the overall prognosis of PTC is favorable, 20–30 % of patients experience disease recurrence, and 5–10 % present with advanced stages at diagnosis [
8
,
9
]. Current therapeutic approaches including surgical resection, radiotherapy, and targeted therapy remain limited in terms of early detection, individualized treatment, and accurate prognostic evaluation [
10
,
11
]. Consequently, there is an urgent need to identify novel molecular targets that can guide the development of more effective therapeutic strategies and improve clinical outcomes for PTC patients.
Apolipoprotein C1 (APOC1) is a small, low-molecular-weight lipoprotein primarily synthesized in the liver [
12
]. Its structural characteristics enable it to bind efficiently to lipids and participate in lipid metabolism and transport. Under physiological conditions,
APOC1
regulates cholesterol homeostasis by inhibiting the activity of cholesterol ester transfer protein (CETP), thereby modulating the synthesis and metabolism of high-density lipoproteins [
13
]. Beyond lipid transport, accumulating evidence indicates that
APOC1
also plays crucial roles in inflammation and immune regulation by influencing cytokine secretion and cellular signaling pathways [
[14]
,
[15]
,
[16]
].
Although previous studies have implicated
APOC1
in the initiation and progression of several malignancies [
[17]
,
[18]
,
[19]
], its precise biological function, regulatory mechanisms, and association with clinicopathological characteristics in PTC remain unclear. A thorough characterization of the expression patterns, clinical relevance, and underlying molecular mechanisms of
APOC1
in PTC may uncover novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets to improve early diagnosis, prognostic prediction, and individualized treatment. Emerging evidence also suggests that aberrant APOC1 expression contributes to remodeling of the tumor microenvironment (TME) and influences immune cell infiltration, emphasizing the importance of investigating its role in PTC immune regulation and potential translational applications.
To elucidate the biological functions and mechanisms of
APOC1
in PTC progression and immune evasion, we adopted a multidimensional research approach. First, we analyzed
APOC1
expression profiles in PTC using publicly available datasets and examined correlations between
APOC1
expression and clinicopathological parameters, including tumor stage, lymph node metastasis, and immune infiltration. We then evaluated the relationship between
APOC1
expression and the composition of immune cells within the tumor microenvironment to determine its potential role in immune regulation. Using molecular docking analyses, we further predicted and validated small-molecule compounds that may directly interact with APOC1. To explore its functional impact, we performed a series of in vitro experiments using PTC cell lines TPC-1 and B-CPAP. We combined 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU) incorporation assays and Ki-67 immunofluorescence staining with colony formation, CCK-8 proliferation, and flow cytometry–based apoptosis analyses. These experiments demonstrated how
APOC1
influences PTC cell proliferation, survival, and resistance to apoptosis, providing mechanistic insights into its contribution to PTC pathogenesis and its potential as a therapeutic target.
Molecular docking and in vitro combination studies demonstrated that cyclopamine, a naturally occurring steroidal alkaloid, acts synergistically with APOC1 inhibition to produce robust antitumor effects in PTC cell models. More importantly, our preliminary in vivo experiments confirmed that cyclopamine effectively suppresses tumor growth in a PTC mouse model. Together, these findings expand our understanding of the biological functions of
APOC1
in PTC and provide both a theoretical framework and preliminary experimental evidence supporting its potential as a diagnostic marker and therapeutic target for individualized treatment and prognosis.
Results
APOC1 is highly expressed in PTC and is associated with poor prognosis
To elucidate the role of
APOC1
in thyroid carcinogenesis, we conducted an integrated bioinformatic analysis using RNA-seq data from the TCGA-THCA project (dbGaP study accession: phs000178) [
20
] accessed through The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database (
https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov
). We extracted transcript-level data in TPM format and visualized
APOC1
expression using the ggplot2 package with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test for statistical evaluation. The dataset included 571 samples, consisting of 59 normal thyroid tissues and 512 thyroid tumor specimens. Our analysis revealed a significant increase in
APOC1
mRNA expression in tumor tissues compared with normal controls (
P
< 0.05).
To validate these results, we integrated data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project, which confirmed that
APOC1
expression was consistently upregulated in malignant thyroid tissues relative to their benign counterparts (
Figs. 1
A–B). Further validation using paired clinical samples showed that
APOC1
expression was markedly higher in thyroid carcinoma tissues than in adjacent non-tumorous tissues (
Fig. 1
C). To evaluate protein-level alterations, we analyzed immunohistochemical (IHC) data from the UALCAN database. Consistent with our transcriptomic results, APOC1 protein abundance was significantly elevated in PTC specimens (
Fig. 1
D). These convergent findings from multiple datasets and experimental platforms underscore the strong association between APOC1 overexpression and papillary thyroid carcinoma.

We further found that
APOC1
expression exhibits strong clinical relevance in PTC. By analyzing filtered RNA-seq data and corresponding clinical information from the TCGA-THCA cohort, we observed that elevated
APOC1
expression positively correlates with advanced tumor stage (
Fig. 2
A) and progressive disease status (
Figs. 2
B–C). In addition,
APOC1
expression was significantly higher in patients aged ≥45 years compared with younger individuals (
Fig. 2
D). Analysis of
APOC1
across different pathological subtypes of PTC revealed that its expression was markedly increased in the classic and tall-cell variants both associated with higher malignancy along with several rarer subtypes, compared with normal thyroid tissues. Furthermore,
APOC1
expression varied significantly according to tumor location (
Fig. 2
F) and the type of primary lesion (
Fig. 2
G). These findings demonstrate that
APOC1
expression patterns are strongly associated with disease stage, tumor progression, patient age, histological subtype, and anatomical site, suggesting that
APOC1
may serve as a potential biomarker for PTC classification and clinical assessment.

Fig 2
Taken together, our data show that
APOC1
expression is markedly elevated in PTC and that higher
APOC1
levels are statistically correlated with poorer patient prognosis.
APOC1
deficiency inhibits aggressive progression in PTC
To investigate the functional role of
APOC1
overexpression, we performed siRNA-mediated knockdown of
APOC1
in TPC-1 and B-CPAP cells. RT-qPCR(
Fig. 1
E) and Western blot(
Fig. 1
G) confirmed efficient silencing, validating the model for downstream assays. Functional analyses showed that
APOC1
depletion markedly suppressed oncogenic behaviors. Cell proliferation measured by the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay was significantly decreased in both TPC-1 and B-CPAP cells compared with siRNA controls (
Fig. 1
F). Consistently, immunofluorescence staining for EdU revealed a reduction in proliferating cells (
Figs. 1
H–I). We further evaluated the effect of
APOC1
silencing on migration using a wound-healing assay.
APOC1
knockdown cells displayed a notably slower wound closure rate than controls (
Fig. 1
J-K). Colony formation assays also showed a pronounced reduction in clonogenic potential in siAPOC1-treated cells (
Fig. 1
L).
Together, these results demonstrate that
APOC1
is essential for sustaining the proliferative, migratory, and survival capacities of papillary thyroid carcinoma cells.
APOC1
induces immune escape in PTC
Given the crucial role of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) in cancer progression and patient outcomes, and the potential involvement of
APOC1
in regulating immune cell infiltration within the tumor microenvironment [
21
], we next examined the relationship between
APOC1
expression and immune cell composition. Using the CIBERSORT algorithm and 22 immune cell markers provided by the CIBERSORTx platform (
https://cibersortx.stanford.edu/
), we quantified immune infiltration patterns in the dataset. Our analysis revealed that
APOC1
overexpression significantly reshapes the immune landscape of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Elevated
APOC1
levels positively correlated with increased infiltration of resting dendritic cells, γδ T cells, M0 and M2 macrophages, and activated memory CD4⁺ T cells (
Figs. 3
A–E). Conversely, high
APOC1
expression was associated with decreased infiltration of activated mast cells, resting and activated NK cells, resting memory CD4⁺ T cells, eosinophils, and monocytes (
Figs. 3
F–M).

These findings suggest that
APOC1
may influence immune evasion in PTC by modulating the tumor immune microenvironment.
Drug prediction and validation for PTC
Although several targeted therapies have been approved for PTC, their high cost and limited accessibility highlight the urgent need for more effective and affordable treatment options. To identify potential small-molecule therapeutics, we utilized the Connectivity Map (CMAP) database (
https://clue.io/
) [
22
] to predict compounds that may target pathways associated with APOC1. We extracted
APOC1
expression data from the TCGA-THCA dataset and stratified samples into high- and low-expression groups. DEGs between these groups were identified using the DESeq2 package (BH-corrected
P
-value < 0.01, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, |LogFC| > 1.5, and
P
adj
< 0.05). These DEGs were subsequently analyzed in the CMAP database to identify candidate compounds with inverse expression signatures. In this analysis, a more negative connectivity score indicated stronger predicted therapeutic potential. We identified eight small-molecule compounds (
Table 1
) with the highest absolute enrichment scores: farnesylthioacetic acid (
Fig. 4
A), papaverine (
Fig. 4
B), hycanthone (
Fig. 4
C), indolophenanthridine (
Fig. 4
D), nicaraven (
Fig. 4
E), methylnorlichexanthone (
Fig. 4
F), fananserin (
Fig. 4
G), and cyclopamine (
Fig. 4
H). These compounds exhibited promising enrichment profiles suggestive of antitumor activity in PTC. To further assess their pharmacological potential, we obtained detailed chemical information and three-dimensional molecular structures from the PubChem database (
Figs. 4
A–F). These structural analyses provide insight into potential mechanisms of action and guide future optimization efforts. We hypothesize that these compounds may exert therapeutic effects by modulating key signaling pathways and molecular targets regulated by APOC1. Collectively, our findings offer a valuable foundation for identifying novel, cost-effective therapeutic candidates for papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Fig 4
We next conducted molecular docking analysis using AutoDock Vina (version 1.1.2) [
23
] to evaluate the binding interactions between the APOC1 protein and eight candidate compounds: farnesylthioacetic acid, papaverine, hycanthone, indolophenanthridine, nicaraven, methylnorlichexanthone, fananserin, and cyclopamine (
Figs. 5
A–
5
H). Among these, the docking of APOC1 with cyclopamine revealed particularly strong binding characteristics. The AutoDock Vina score of −7.9 indicated a high binding affinity, with lower (more negative) values reflecting stronger interactions. This strong affinity suggests that cyclopamine can spontaneously bind to APOC1 and may modulate related biological pathways, including inhibition of the oncogenic Hedgehog signaling pathway. The calculated binding pocket volume of 219 Å³ demonstrates sufficient spatial capacity to accommodate small-molecule ligands such as cyclopamine, underscoring its potential as a lead compound for developing targeted pharmacological interventions against papillary thyroid carcinoma. The coordinates of the identified binding site (17, 4, −5) define its precise three-dimensional location on the APOC1 protein, providing a critical reference for future experimental validation and computational modeling. The docking grid dimensions (24 × 24 × 24 Å) indicate the spatial extent used during simulation, ensuring full coverage of the potential ligand-binding pocket across all axes. Key interacting residues, VAL12, SER15, ILE16, VAL17, GLU19, GLY20, PRO21, ALA22, PRO23, ALA24, GLY26, THR27, PRO28, ASP29, VAL30, SER32, ALA33, LEU34, LYS36, LEU37, and PHE40, were identified as potential contact points forming stable interactions with the ligand. These residues likely constitute critical hotspots that mediate the binding of small molecules to APOC1.

Among all tested compounds, APOC1 exhibited measurable binding affinity with each; however, cyclopamine showed the lowest binding energy (
Fig. 5
H), indicating the strongest predicted interaction and highest potential for specific APOC1 targeting in papillary thyroid carcinoma.
Cyclopamine inhibits proliferation and induces apoptosis in PTC cells
To further elucidate the antitumor effects of cyclopamine on PTC, we first examined its impact on cell proliferation using Ki-67 immunofluorescence staining. TPC-1 cells were treated with cyclopamine at concentrations of 0 μM, 10 μM, and 20 μM. The results demonstrated a marked, dose-dependent decrease in Ki-67-positive cells, indicating that cyclopamine significantly suppressed cellular proliferation (
Figs. 6
A–B). These findings suggest that cyclopamine effectively inhibits the expression of proliferation-associated markers in PTC cells. We next assessed the dynamic proliferative response using the CCK-8 assay. Treatment with increasing concentrations of cyclopamine (0 μM, 10 μM, 20 μM, and 40 μM) resulted in a clear, concentration-dependent reduction in the proliferation of both TPC-1 and B-CPAP cell lines (
Figs. 6
C–D). To explore the mechanism underlying this antiproliferative effect, we evaluated apoptosis using Annexin V-FITC/PI double staining and flow cytometry. As cyclopamine concentration increased, apoptosis rates rose significantly in both cell lines (
Fig. 6
E), confirming that the compound suppresses tumor growth at least in part by inducing apoptosis. Finally, the colony formation assay further validated the long-term antiproliferative capacity of cyclopamine. After 14 days of treatment with 10 μM and 20 μM cyclopamine, both TPC-1 and B-CPAP cells exhibited a substantial reduction in colony number, with nearly complete inhibition observed at 20 μM.

Collectively, these results demonstrate that cyclopamine exerts potent, multidimensional antitumor activity in PTC by dose-dependently suppressing proliferation, promoting apoptosis, and inhibiting colony formation, thereby establishing its therapeutic potential for papillary thyroid carcinoma.
APOC1
knockdown coupled with cyclopamine exhibits synergistic effects for inhibiting PTC
To assess the in vitro antiproliferative efficacy of combined si-APOC1 and cyclopamine treatment in PTC cell lines and to determine whether this combination produces a synergistic effect, we performed apoptosis analysis using Annexin V-FITC/PI double-staining flow cytometry. Compared with either single treatment or the control group, the combined si-APOC1 and cyclopamine treatment markedly increased apoptosis in both TPC-1 and B-CPAP cells (
Fig. 7
A), indicating a strong pro-apoptotic effect of the combination therapy. To further evaluate its long-term impact on cell proliferation, we conducted colony formation assays. The results were consistent with the apoptosis analysis: relative to either monotherapy or the control group, combined si-APOC1 and cyclopamine treatment significantly reduced colony-forming ability in both cell lines (
Figs. 7
B–C). This pronounced reduction in colony number and size demonstrates that the combination persistently suppresses cellular proliferation and tumorigenic potential, reflecting severe impairment of self-renewal and replicative capacity. These findings suggest that the enhanced therapeutic effect of this combination may result from the simultaneous activation of apoptotic pathways and inhibition of proliferative signaling.

Collectively, our data indicate that co-targeting APOC1 with cyclopamine exerts a potent synergistic antitumor effect in vitro, providing a strong rationale for further in vivo validation and mechanistic investigation of this combination strategy as a promising therapeutic approach for papillary thyroid carcinoma.
Cyclopamine inhibits tumor growth in the PTC mouse model
To evaluate the in vivo antitumor efficacy of cyclopamine in PTC, we established a subcutaneous xenograft model using TPC-1 cells in mice (
Fig. 8
A). IHC staining for Ki-67 and TUNEL assays revealed that cyclopamine markedly suppressed tumor cell proliferation and angiogenesis (
Fig. 8
B). Cyclopamine was administered intraperitoneally every two days, leading to significantly reduced tumor volume (
Figs. 8
D–E) and final tumor weight (
Fig. 8
F) compared with the control group (
P
< 0.05). Although cyclopamine significantly inhibited tumor growth, no notable differences in body weight were observed between treated and control mice (
Fig. 8
F), suggesting minimal systemic toxicity. Moreover, histological examination showed no evident damage to major organs, including the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys (
Fig. 8
H).

Collectively, these findings demonstrate that cyclopamine effectively suppresses PTC xenograft growth in vivo without causing observable systemic toxicity, providing strong preclinical support for its potential therapeutic application in papillary thyroid carcinoma.
Discussion
Thyroid cancer, predominantly PTC, is the most common endocrine malignancy worldwide, with its incidence rising steadily and a noticeable shift toward younger patient populations [
24
,
25
]. Although PTC generally carries a favorable prognosis [
26
,
27
], a subset of patients develops aggressive or metastatic disease, which markedly reduces survival rates [
28
,
29
].
APOC1
, a key low-molecular-weight lipoprotein, has recently been implicated in tumor progression across multiple malignancies [
[30]
,
[31]
,
[32]
]; however, its biological role and clinical significance in thyroid carcinoma remain poorly understood.
Accumulating evidence indicates that
APOC1
plays a crucial role in the initiation, progression, and metastasis of several cancers, including gastric, pancreatic, cervical, and renal carcinomas [
19
,
33
,
34
]. It promotes tumor cell proliferation, migration, and invasion and is often associated with unfavorable patient outcomes. Notably, recent studies have shown that
APOC1
is predominantly expressed in tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) within the tumor microenvironment [
34
]. This elevated expression appears to contribute to immune regulation by influencing macrophage polarization. Specifically,
APOC1
overexpression enhances the expression of CD163 and CD206, driving macrophages toward the M2 phenotype—a state commonly linked to tumor-promoting immunosuppression and malignant progression. Such M2 polarization enables cancer cells to evade immune surveillance while simultaneously fostering tumor growth, angiogenesis, and metastasis [
35
]. Together, these findings suggest that
APOC1
not only participates in tumor cell–intrinsic oncogenic signaling but may also exert a broader immunomodulatory role within the tumor microenvironment, positioning it as a promising candidate for targeted therapeutic intervention in PTC.
Our findings demonstrate that elevated
APOC1
expression correlates with advanced tumor lymph node metastasis (TNM) stages (III and IV) and poorer pathological grades (
Fig. 2
). We further observed that
APOC1
overexpression in PTC positively associates with both M0 and M2 macrophage populations. Although M0 macrophages are typically considered non-polarized, their relationship with
APOC1
suggests a transitional state that precedes polarization. We propose that high
APOC1
expression in PTC promotes macrophage polarization toward the immunosuppressive M2 phenotype, thereby enhancing tumor immune evasion. Consistent with our findings, single-cell analyses in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) have revealed that
APOC1
is highly expressed in TAMs. Inhibition of
APOC1
expression facilitates the conversion of M2 to M1 macrophages through the ferroptosis pathway, remodeling the tumor immune microenvironment and improving the response to anti-PD1 immunotherapy [
36
].
Cyclopamine, a steroidal alkaloid extracted from Veratrum californicum, functions as a natural antagonist of the Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway [
[37]
,
[38]
,
[39]
]. In several malignancies, including colorectal and gastric cancers, Cyclopamine has shown synergistic effects when combined with conventional chemotherapeutic agents [
40
,
41
]. These combinations enhance therapeutic efficacy and help overcome drug resistance [
42
,
43
]. Furthermore, Cyclopamine suppresses cancer stem cell activity, a property with significant clinical relevance for preventing tumor recurrence and metastasis [
[44]
,
[45]
,
[46]
].
Our findings demonstrate that Cyclopamine suppresses thyroid cancer cell proliferation in a dose-dependent manner, promotes apoptosis, and inhibits clonal expansion, collectively exerting broad and potent anti-tumor effects. Despite these promising results, the absence of a functional immune system in current animal models represents a major limitation, constraining their utility in cancer immunology research and in the preclinical evaluation of immunomodulatory therapies. Furthermore, the intricate composition of the tumor microenvironment may influence the true contribution of
APOC1
deficiency to Cyclopamine’s anti-cancer activity. To address these challenges, future studies should include larger sample sizes and incorporate comprehensive clinical datasets to enhance the robustness, reproducibility, and translational relevance of the findings.
In conclusion, our study highlights APOC1 as a promising therapeutic target and underscores the significant anti-cancer potential of Cyclopamine in PTC. These results provide important insights into developing novel therapeutic strategies and advancing precision oncology. Further investigations should elucidate the synergistic mechanisms between APOC1 suppression and Cyclopamine treatment and assess their interactions with other therapeutic modalities. Such efforts could lead to innovative, personalized treatment approaches for thyroid cancer and improved clinical outcomes for patients.
Materials and methods
Cell culture
Human papillary thyroid carcinomas cell lines TPC-1 and B-CPAP were procured from Biotechnology Co., Ltd. Of cellcook (Guang Zhou, China). TPC-1 were cultivated in RPMI-1640 medium (Invitrogen, 11,875,093) with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Gibco, 10,099,141). B-CPAP were cultivated in RPMI-1640 medium (Invitrogen, 11,875,093) with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Gibco, 10,099,141), 1 % NEAA (Invitrogen 11,140,050), 1 % Glutamax (Invitrogen 35,050,061), 1 %Sodium Pyruvate 100 mM Solution (Invitrogen 11,360,070) and 100 U/ml penicillin/streptomycin at a temperature of 37 °C and 5 % CO2. Cyclopamine (APExBIO. A8340) and CCK-8 reagent were purchased from APExBIO.Edu (C0071S) were purchased from Beyotime.
Mouse model
All animal experiments were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Naval Medical University, Shanghai, China (approval ID: NMUMREC-2025–055). BALB/c mice aged 6 to 8 weeks used in the experiment were purchased from Shanghai Laboratory Animal Research Center (SLARC). A total of 2 × 10^
6
TPC-1 thyroid papillary carcinoma cells suspended in 0.2 mL PBS (PBS: Matrigel=1:1) were implanted subcutaneously into the right side of the mice. When the tumor volume reached 50 to 100 mm^
3
, the mice were randomly divided into four groups (five mice each group). The Cyclopamine treatment group was administered 25 mg/kg Cyclopamine via intraperitoneal injection every two days for 20 days. The control group received 0.9 % NaCl via intraperitoneal injection. Throughout the treatment period, the body weight and tumor size of each mouse were recorded every three days. Tumor volume was calculated using the formula
V
= (width)^
2
× length / 2. At the end of the experiment, the mice were euthanized, and the tumors and selected organ tissues were quickly separated and weighed.
CCK-8 assay
For cell proliferation assay, TPC-1 or B-CPAP cells (1 × 10
5
cells/well) were plated in 96-well plates exposed to different concentrations of Cyclopamine. At 0, 24, 48 and 72 h post-treatment, cells were collected and cell proliferation was evaluated by CCK-8 assay kit (Beyotime, China).
Colony formation assay
In each well of a 6-well plate, 1000 cells were seeded and treated with Cyclopamine (10 μM) or siAPOC1 sequences for 14 days. After 14 days of treatment, visible clones were observed. After fixation with 4 % paraformaldehyde (PFA) at room temperature for 30 min, cells were stained with crystal violet solution (Beyotime, China). The number of clones was counted, and images were collected.
Wound-healing assay
TPC-1 and B-CPAP cells into a 12-well plate. When the cell confluence reaches about 90 %, use a 20 μL pipette tip to create vertical scratches in the center of each well. Then, gently wash three times with PBS to remove the detached cells. Following the washing step, add siAPOC1 solution at the specified concentration to the wells and continue culturing the cells. Observe the changes in scratch widths by microscopy after 24 h to assess the effect of cell migration ability.
Apoptosis analysis
The apoptosis detection kit (MultiSciences BioTech) was used to evaluate the effects of Cyclopamine and siAPOC1 treatments on apoptosis in TPC-1 and B-CPAP cells. A suspension containing 1 × 10^6 cells was gently mixed with 5 μL Annexin V-FITC solution and 10 μL PI staining solution, then incubated in the dark on ice for 5 min. Fluorescence analysis was subsequently performed using flow cytometry.
Molecular docking
The structure of APOC1 protein comes from the RCSB PDB database (
https://www.pdbus.org/
), in PDB format. Farnesylthioacetic-acid; Papaverine; Hycanthone; Indolophenanthridine; Nicaraven; Methylnorlichexanthone; Fananserin and Cyclopamine. The three-dimensional structure comes from the PubChem database (
https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/
), in MOL2 file format. Molecular docking is performed using Autodock Vina software, evaluating the stability of the receptor and ligand binding through binding energy.
Real-time PCR (qRT-PCR)
Total RNA was extracted from cells using an RNA extraction kit (Fastagen). The RNA concentration was measured in ng/μL using a NanoDrop 2000 (Thermo Scientific). cDNA was synthesized using a reverse transcription kit (Accurate BioTech) for qPCR. Quantitative PCR detection was then performed using Fast qPCR Mix (Accurate BioTech, catalog number [please insert catalog number]). The expression levels of the target gene were normalized using GAPDH as an internal reference. The primer sequences used in this study are as follows:
APOC1
, forward primer: TCCAGTGCCTTGGATAAGCTG; reverse primer: GGCTGATGAGTTCCCGAGC;
GAPDH, forward primer: ACAACTTTGGTATCGTGGAAGG; reverse primer: GCCATCACGCCACAGTTTC.
Western blotting analysis
The harvested cells were lysed in cell lysis buffer (Beyeyotime, P0013B) to obtain a complete cell lysate. The protein concentration was evaluated using the BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Fisher, A55865). Equal amounts of protein from each sample were loaded for electrophoresis via SDS-PAGE. And proteins were transferred onto nitrocellulose (NC) membranes. Subsequently, the NC membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies APOC1 (Abcam, ab198288) and GAPDH (Proteintech, 6004). Followed by incubation secondary antibodies under appropriate conditions. Immunoreactive bands were analysis of the Western blot was using ImageJ software.
Transfection
For the
APOC1
knockdown experiment,
APOC1
siRNA was synthesized by Sangon Shanghai Technology. The sequences of
APOC1
siRNAs and negative control siRNAs are as follows: siAPOC1
#
1: GAAACACACUGGAGGACAATT,UUGUCCUCCAGUGUGUUUCTT; siAPOC1
#
2:CAUCAAAAGAGUGGAACUUTT,AAGUUCCACUCUUUUGAUGTT;siAPOC1
#
3:AGAAAGUGAAGGAAGAAACUTT,AGUUUCUUCCUUCACUUUCUTT; control siRNAs: forward primer UUCUCCGAACGUGUCACGUTT; reverse primer: ACGUGACACGUUCGGAGAATT. Briefly, cell culture was performed in a 6-well plate. After 12 h of cell culture, siRNA was transfected into the cells using the transfection reagent jet PRIME (catalog number 101,000,046).
Immunofluorescence
Using the EdU cell proliferation detection kit (Beyotime, China) to evaluate cell proliferation by detecting cell DNA synthesis. Cells were seeded at 5 × 10^
5
cells per well in a 12-well plate. Pre-warmed EdU (20 μM, 37 °C) was added to the culture medium, and incubation was performed for 2 h to complete EdU labeling. Subsequently, cells were fixed with 4 % paraformaldehyde (PFA) and permeabilized with Triton X-100 (Beyotime, China) for 20 min, followed by the addition of click reaction solution and Hoechst nuclear staining. Quantitative analysis of EdU-positive cells was performed using a confocal laser scanning microscope imaging system (CLSM600, China).
Using the Ki-67 cell proliferation detection kit (Beyotime, China), cells were seeded at 5 × 10^5 cells per well in a 12-well plate, fixed with 4 % paraformaldehyde (PFA) and permeabilized with Triton X-100 for 20 min, and then blocked with 10 % blocking solution at room temperature for 0.5 h. Subsequently, the cells were incubated overnight with the primary antibody Ki-67 antibody at 4 °C. The cells were stained with Alexa Fluor 647 labeled secondary antibody (Proteintech) and counterstained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) (
D21490
, Thermo Fisher) for the nuclei. Quantitative analysis of Ki-67 positive cells was performed using a confocal microscopy imaging system (CLSM600, China).
Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 20.0 and GraphPad Prism 10, Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) from at least three independent experiments. Comparisons between multiple groups were conducted using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s post hoc test. For non-normal data, nonparametric tests, such as the Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn’s post hoc test, were applied. Differences were considered statistically significant at
P
< 0.05, denoted as *
P
< 0.05, **
P
< 0.01, and *
P
< 0.001. Correlation analyses between experimental outcomes, docking binding energies, and gene expression levels were performed using Pearson or Spearman correlation coefficients, depending on data distribution.
